title: The White Boxes Had Not Grown Heavier
teaser: The materials and labor for 120 white boxes checked out exactly, and the old cost sheet still showed an attractive margin. What changed the quotation were the support activities behind the job order—the ones that had not become fewer just because the batch contained only 100 boxes.
paragraphs: At 4:20 on Friday afternoon, Zhou Min had only one renewal order left on her desk: 120 white gift boxes. The customer wanted last month's price, and sales needed an answer before five. The cost sheet seemed straightforward. For three months, the white box had shown a higher accounting margin than the standard black box. But the workshop had clipped a setup record behind the job order and asked her to look again. Zhou Min began with the places where errors were easiest to make. Direct material cost was 20 yuan per black box and 24 yuan per white box; direct labor was 10 yuan and 12 yuan respectively. Material issues, returns, clocked labor, and completed quantities all reconciled.

Under the old method, the month's 1,000 yuan of manufacturing overhead was spread evenly across 1,100 finished boxes, or about 0.91 yuan per box. The 1,000 black boxes therefore absorbed about 909 yuan, while the 100 white boxes absorbed only about 91 yuan. The method had been used for years, and it had not been irrational. In the past, the workshop usually ran long batches of the same product once a machine was set up. Larger volume generally came with more setups, purchasing, and receiving support as well, so output and support work moved roughly together. Averaging by units rarely pushed the apparent costs of the two products very far apart.

Zhou Min turned to the setup record. It contained only two lines: black boxes, 2 setups; white boxes, 8 setups. The purchasing records showed the same pattern—2 purchase orders and 8. Although there were only 100 white boxes, four types of lining and different foil-stamped lettering had split them into several small batches. Every change required clearing material, adjusting fixtures, and testing a first piece. Every purchase order required a quotation, system entry, and receiving check. She pulled the records for the previous three months as well. Each setup had taken roughly the standard workshop time; no particular operator was unusually slow. Yet the white boxes consistently generated far more setups and purchase orders than the black ones.

She separated the month's 1,000 yuan of support cost into two stacks according to the records: 600 yuan for setup support and 400 yuan for purchasing and receiving support. There had been ten setups in total, so each setup represented 60 yuan. There had also been ten purchase orders, so each one represented 40 yuan. The black boxes therefore absorbed 2×60 plus 2×40, or 200 yuan. The white boxes absorbed 8×60 plus 8×40, or 800 yuan. The total was still 1,000 yuan; not a single yuan had been added. The difference was that the cost no longer went first through an average across 1,100 boxes. It went first to the activities that had actually occurred, and then to the products that had caused them.

At 4:42, sales came back for an answer. Zhou Min tried one more allocation based on direct labor cost. The numbers moved somewhat, but the method still could not explain why 100 white boxes triggered eight setups and eight purchase orders. She did not reject the order for 120 boxes. Instead, she offered two quotations. If the customer kept four combinations, the relevant activity costs would remain in the price. If the lining and foil lettering were consolidated into two combinations, the quantity would still be 120, but fewer support activities would be required. The customer kept the quantity and chose two combinations.

After the 120 boxes were finished, neither material use nor labor per unit showed anything unusual. The workshop, however, had carried out three fewer setups and three fewer small purchase orders than under the previous combination. The white box no longer showed the unusually strong margin seen on the old sheet, while the black box's margin moved somewhat higher. When Zhou Min filed the job, she clipped the original record back behind the work order. It did not say 'expensive' or 'cheap.' It contained only the same two old lines: black boxes, 2 setups; white boxes, 8.
concept: The core of activity-based costing (ABC) is that resources are consumed by activities, and cost objects in turn consume resources by causing those activities. When products differ substantially in batch size, complexity, setups, purchasing, inspection, or other activity frequency, allocating overhead only by output volume or another single scale measure can create systematic cross-subsidies: low-volume, high-complexity products may be understated, while high-volume, simple products may be overstated.
explanation: The story first shows why the old method once had a reasonable baseline: production used to be homogeneous and run in long batches, so output and support activities moved roughly together. The white box was later split into many small batches by multiple specifications, changing its activity structure while the allocation rule stayed the same. Direct materials, direct labor, completed quantities, and material movements all reconcile, and setup times remain within the standard range, which rules out missing records and inefficient execution. A second allocation based on direct labor still cannot explain the gap between two and eight activities. Finally, the customer keeps the quantity at 120 but reduces the number of combinations, and actual setups and purchase orders fall. That outcome further shows that the cost difference comes from activity frequency rather than output volume alone or worker efficiency.
mapping: When production previously ran in long batches, support work changed roughly with volume → simple volume-based allocation once had an acceptable normal baseline.

Only 100 white boxes generate 8 setups and 8 purchase orders, while each setup stays within standard time → the higher support cost comes from activity frequency, not missing materials or inefficient execution.
The 1,000 yuan is first divided into a 600-yuan setup pool and a 400-yuan purchasing pool, then assigned using 2 versus 8 activities → this shows the ABC chain of resources → activities → products.

In the later order, quantity remains 120 while combinations fall from four to two, and both setups and small purchase orders fall by three → the actual operating result confirms that complexity drives activities rather than volume itself.
boundary: ABC is not more accurate simply because it is more detailed. Activity pools, driver records, and system maintenance all cost money, and weak or unstable cost drivers can create new distortions. If processes are highly homogeneous and overhead is small, a simple allocation may already be sufficient. ABC improves the match between overhead and resource consumption; by itself, it does not decide whether a product should be repriced, retained, discontinued, or negotiated differently with a customer.
reflection: If the next batch still contains 120 white boxes but the combinations fall from two to one, would you look first at the quantity produced, or at how the number of setups, purchase orders, and other activities changes?
